feed.title: Web & Frontend — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Front-End Checklist
entry.summary: A checklist of items to verify before launching a web page across HTML, CSS, JS, accessibility, performance and SEO, with priority labels. Unlike general guides it is a tickable, prioritised checklist.

entry.title: Mozilla Web Security Guidelines
entry.summary: Mozilla's recommended security headers and settings for websites: CSP, HSTS, cookie flags, CORS, SRI. It gives a priority and an example configuration for each, making it more actionable than general security articles.

entry.title: NGINX Config Generator (nginxconfig.io)
entry.summary: A form-driven generator that builds a ready NGINX config from domain, PHP/Node, security and performance options. Compared with copying sample configs, it adds best-practice settings (TLS, headers, gzip) automatically.

entry.title: Protomaps
entry.summary: An open-source map stack that serves a world basemap as a single PMTiles file; the file sits on plain storage such as S3 and the browser reads only the parts it needs through HTTP range requests. Unlike hosted map services such as Mapbox there is no tile server and no per-use fee.

entry.title: The A11Y Project
entry.summary: A community-run accessibility site with a plain checklist based on WCAG, articles and lists of tools and resources. Unlike the W3C quick reference it states the criteria as items a developer can follow rather than in standards language.

entry.title: WAVE
entry.summary: WebAIM’s accessibility evaluation tool; given an address, or through its browser extension, it overlays errors, alerts and structural information as icons on the page. Unlike scanners that produce a report it shows each problem in place on the page; the extension also checks pages behind a login, locally.

entry.title: WCAG 2.2 Hızlı Başvuru
entry.summary: The W3C’s “How to Meet WCAG” page: every success criterion, its level (A, AA, AAA), the techniques that satisfy it and the common failures, filterable by level and topic. Unlike reading the standard itself it takes you from a criterion straight to a technique you can apply.

entry.title: WebAssembly
entry.summary: The official site of the WebAssembly standard: the specifications, an introduction to the concepts and a feature table showing which proposal is supported in which browser and runtime. Unlike MDN’s WebAssembly pages it looks from the standard and the runtimes rather than from the JavaScript side.

entry.title: webhint
entry.summary: An open-source linter that scans a site for accessibility, speed, security and compatibility problems and explains each rule; it runs as an online scan, a CLI and a VS Code extension. Unlike Lighthouse it documents every rule in detail and is configurable.

entry.title: ni
entry.summary: One command that picks npm, yarn, pnpm or bun for each project from its lockfile. Unlike remembering which manager a repo uses you type the same thing everywhere.

entry.title: Awesome Angular
entry.summary: A list of components, tools and tutorials for the Angular application framework. Unlike the official docs it gathers community libraries and real examples.

entry.title: Awesome ESLint
entry.summary: A list of plugins and configs for ESLint, the JavaScript linter. Unlike the ESLint docs, it gathers community-shared configs and plugins specific to frameworks such as React and Vue.

entry.title: Awesome Frontend GIS
entry.summary: A list of libraries for geographic information systems (maps) in the browser. Unlike general mapping-API lists, it focuses on libraries that run in the browser rather than on a server — rendering, data conversion, spatial analysis.

entry.title: Awesome HTML5
entry.summary: A list of HTML5 APIs — Canvas, WebSocket, storage — plus tools and resources. Unlike general web lists, it focuses only on the browser APIs that came with the HTML5 standard.

entry.title: Awesome Mobile Web Development
entry.summary: A resource list for building a good mobile web experience — touch events, performance, offline. Unlike native-app lists, it targets mobile sites running in the browser.

entry.title: Awesome npm
entry.summary: A list of tips, tools and resources for npm, the Node package manager. Unlike the npm docs, it gathers the tools around it — package search sites, publishing helpers, CLI add-ons.

entry.title: Awesome npm scripts
entry.summary: A resource list for using npm scripts as a task runner. Unlike task runners such as Gulp or Grunt, it teaches making do with package.json scripts and no extra dependency.

entry.title: Awesome Ponyfills
entry.summary: A list of ponyfill libraries that add native behaviour without overriding it. Unlike polyfills they never patch globals: you import the feature as a separate module.

entry.title: Awesome Preact
entry.summary: A list of components, tools and examples for Preact, the 3 KB lightweight React alternative. Unlike React lists, it collects only libraries that work with Preact and keep its small size.

entry.title: Awesome React
entry.summary: A list of libraries, tools and learning resources for the React ecosystem. Unlike the official docs, it gathers the surrounding ecosystem — state management, routing, component libraries, testing — in one list.

entry.title: Awesome React Hooks
entry.summary: A list of libraries, examples and articles for React Hooks. Unlike general React lists, it gathers only hook-based patterns and custom-hook packages, not class components.

entry.title: Awesome Standard
entry.summary: A resource list for Standard, the zero-config JS style guide and linter. Unlike configuring ESLint by hand, the rules are fixed and not up for debate; the list gathers editor plugins and compatible tools.

entry.title: Awesome Svelte
entry.summary: A list of components and tools for Svelte and SvelteKit. Unlike React-heavy lists it shows the ecosystem specific to this compile-time framework.

entry.title: Awesome WebExtensions
entry.summary: A resource list for building cross-browser add-ons (WebExtensions). Unlike single-browser docs it focuses on the common API that works across Chrome, Firefox and Safari.

entry.title: Awesome WebXR
entry.summary: A resource list for WebXR, enabling virtual/augmented reality in the browser. Unlike native XR SDKs, these experiences open in a browser with nothing to install; the list gathers frameworks, samples and tools.

entry.title: Awesome WP-CLI
entry.summary: A resource list for WP-CLI, managing WordPress from the command line. Unlike the admin dashboard it offers bulk, scriptable operations: updating plugins on a hundred sites is one command.

entry.title: Browser Diet
entry.summary: A guide of concrete tips for improving web performance. Unlike automated audits such as Lighthouse, the advice is hand-written by experts with its reasoning; part of it dates from the HTTP/1 era.

entry.title: Can I email…
entry.summary: A table showing which email client supports an HTML/CSS feature. Unlike the web’s Can I use it looks at the quirky, limited support of email clients.

entry.title: Chart.js
entry.summary: A JavaScript library drawing simple, responsive charts on canvas. Unlike heavy visualisation libraries it is lightweight and works in a few lines.

entry.title: DevSamples
entry.summary: Ready-to-copy HTML, CSS and JavaScript code examples. Unlike documentation, it gives small working snippets rather than explanations.

entry.title: docsify
entry.summary: A tool turning Markdown files into a documentation site in the browser, with no build. Unlike static generators it has no build step — it serves the pages on the fly.

entry.title: Firefox Developer Edition
entry.summary: A build of Firefox for web developers, with advanced debugging tools built in. Unlike Chrome DevTools, its CSS Grid and Flexbox inspectors and its fonts panel are notably strong.

entry.title: Frontend Focus
entry.summary: A newsletter rounding up frontend news, articles and tools weekly. Unlike scattered following it gives a single, filtered digest.

entry.title: Frontend Mentor
entry.summary: A practice platform that gives realistic design files and asks you to turn them into code. Unlike random projects it comes with professional designs and community feedback.

entry.title: Joomla
entry.summary: An open-source content management system (CMS), an alternative to WordPress.

entry.title: Patterns.dev
entry.summary: A free resource explaining design and rendering patterns for modern web apps with examples. Unlike classic design-pattern books, it also covers rendering patterns — SSR, static generation, hydration, islands.

entry.title: React Hook Form
entry.summary: A library managing React forms with minimal re-renders and built-in validation. Unlike controlled components it keeps performance high and simplifies the code.

entry.title: Smashing Magazine
entry.summary: In-depth articles, books and practical guides on web design and development. Unlike short blog posts, it publishes long, editor-reviewed articles.

entry.title: SweetAlert2
entry.summary: A library replacing the browser’s ugly alert box with pretty, customisable modals. Unlike the built-in alert it supports styling, input fields and promises.

entry.title: web.dev
entry.summary: Google’s guides and measurement tools for web quality — performance, accessibility, PWA. Unlike MDN it is a guide rather than a reference, explaining metrics such as Core Web Vitals and how to improve them.
